# Sentence-preserving scientific expression guide

This is the shared engineering text for Article and Review sentence editing. Use it only for a request to improve expression within an existing sentence. The Article and Review packages each carry a self-contained copy; no installed Skill must reach into another Skill folder. Scientific and permission contracts still govern application.

## Decide whether a sentence needs editing

Identify the sentence's job before changing its wording. An already clear sentence may remain unchanged. Prefer a precise subject and verb, an explicit referent when context resolves it, and modifiers adjacent to the claim they qualify. Remove avoidable repetition only when every distinct proposition remains. Neither longer syntax nor specialized vocabulary is an improvement by itself.

Check the meaning-bearing fields present in, or directly affected by, the sentence: actor or subject; action or relation; object; model or population; intervention; comparator; endpoint; condition and time; direction and magnitude; negation; uncertainty and causal status; numbers, units, statistics and citation attachment. Do not fill in absent fields. If a field needed for the proposed edit has more than one plausible interpretation, ask about that field instead of choosing one. The proposed sentence must preserve all supplied values and logical relations. Do not merge, split, move or delete sentences for a same-sentence request.

## Match wording to the sentence's evidentiary job

| Job | Useful expression choice | Preserve and avoid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definition | State the term's class and differentiating property close together when both are supplied. | Do not broaden or narrow the defined object or add an unsupplied property. |
| Process | Name the actor, operation and object; make temporal order legible when it matters. | “Enables”, “facilitates”, “causes” and “is associated with” have different strengths. |
| Reported result | Place the measured endpoint near the verb and keep model, condition, comparator and magnitude attached. | Do not turn a reported measurement into a general biological conclusion. |
| Comparison | Use parallel grammatical frames when the two arms truly share a measured dimension. Name the comparison basis. | Do not treat different models, doses, endpoints or reference groups as interchangeable. |
| Association | Use observational language appropriate to the supplied design. | Association does not become mechanism or causation through a stronger verb. |
| Explanation | Separate an observation from a proposed explanation within the sentence when the source does so. | Keep “may”, “suggests”, “is consistent with” and similar limits at their original scope. |
| Negative or null finding | Say which endpoint was not detected or did not differ under which test. | Non-detection is not absence; non-significance is not equivalence or proof of no effect. |
| Limitation | Attach a missing control, detection limit or model boundary to the exact inference it limits. | Do not delete a distinct boundary as repetitive caution or convert it into a positive claim. |

Professional domain collocations are conditional examples, not find-and-replace rules. Preserve the manuscript's exact term identity: “recipient cells” may not mean “target cells”, and “governs” may not mean “influences”. Retain figures, citation identities and placement, statistics, units and abbreviations under the applicable producer contract.

## Concrete English expression choices

These are editorial examples, not scientific findings or a style quota. Use an operation only when the original sentence and its immediate context establish the same actor, relation and referent.

- Put the known actor next to its action: `Protein expression by the cells increased after RNA delivery.` → `After RNA delivery, the cells expressed more protein.` Use this example only when the manuscript explicitly defines the expression endpoint as protein quantity. Otherwise retain the stated expression readout; fluorescence or the fraction of expressing cells does not by itself mean more protein. Keep `after`; do not silently make the delivery a proven cause.
- Keep comparable arms grammatically parallel: `Output increased with A, whereas a decrease in output was observed with B.` → `Output increased with A, whereas it decreased with B.` Retain each arm's actual model, endpoint and comparator.
- Attach a measurement time to the measured outcome: `Protein output, measured with assay X, was higher in treated cells at 24 h than in controls.` → `At 24 h, protein output measured with assay X was higher in treated cells than in controls.` Use this only when the original `24 h` measures output rather than dosing or sample preparation.
- Replace an unclear pronoun with its established referent when context makes the referent unique. Leave the sentence or ask when two referents remain plausible.

A more technical word is useful only if its relation, scope and customary object match the original. Do not change certainty or causal status to make a sentence sound more polished.


## Review the candidate

Compare original and candidate side by side. Check clarity and natural usage separately from meaning preservation; a smoother sentence fails if it changes a protected proposition. Explain a useful change briefly when review is requested. If the sentence has no safe local improvement, keep it and report any structural, evidence or interpretation issue separately.

A corpus-derived expression note may suggest a form only with its source locator, applicability and counterexample. M01 deterministic length or marker statistics cannot establish a preferred collocation, rhetorical role or semantic equivalence. Treat model-assisted corpus observations and editor judgments as distinct from admitted M01 profile features. A project-specific Review note must not silently become Article guidance.
